guide.intro: Pick how you want to use Unslop — both paths end at your first scan result. The progress below is derived live from your account.

github.installApp: The GitHub App posts reviews as native checks on your pull requests. Install it once for your account or organization and choose which repositories it may see.
github.activateRepo: Activating a repository registers it with the Gatekeeper and starts a one-time index of its API surface. Only activated repositories are reviewed.
github.openPr: From now on every pull request is reviewed automatically — findings land as a check run and as review comments on the PR.

cli.installCli: The CLI runs the same review pipeline against your local changes, before anything reaches a pull request.

cli.firstScan: Scans your tracked changes against the merge-base and prints the findings in the terminal — zero configuration.

guide.extensionBody: The extension shows findings directly in the editor and lets you review and apply fixes without leaving it. It uses the same sign-in as the CLI.
guide.extensionInstall: Install it from the VS Code Marketplace and click the shield in the status bar to scan.
guide.ciNote: CI note: unslop scan exits with a non-zero code when a CRITICAL finding is confirmed — the build fails.

meta.title: Unslop — Review gate for AI-generated code
meta.description: Unslop reviews AI-generated code on every pull request: deterministic checks first, then a model review whose findings a second model re-checks blind. Every finding names its rule. In private beta.
meta.ogTagline: Deterministic checks first. Model findings re-checked blind. Skipped stages reported.

hero.headline: Looks fine in review. <accent>Breaks in production.</accent>
hero.bluf: Unslop reviews every pull request for the ways AI-written code fails: swallowed errors, packages that don’t exist, SQL built from strings, tests that assert nothing.
hero.sub: A deterministic pre-scan runs first. Then a model reviews the diff, and a second model re-checks its findings without seeing the first one’s reasoning. Every finding names its rule and quotes the code.
hero.status: Private beta. Sign-up is closed, and the CLI, the editor extension and the MCP server are not published yet.
hero.tagline: Show the finding. Explain the verdict. Say what was skipped.
hero.exhibitCaption: Real output, not a mock-up: the check run and the review comment on pull request #20 in our own test repository, 2026-09-30. This finding comes from the deterministic pre-scan.

findings.heading: Two more findings, copied as stored
findings.intro: Both come from scans of our own test repository. Rule, quoted code, explanation and fix are product output, unedited. The product writes its findings in English.

confirmed.label: Model finding, confirmed by the blind re-check
confirmed.caption: CLI scan of 2026-09-17, job 0cf82b14. The reviewing model drafted the finding. The second model confirmed it from the rule and the quoted code alone.

downgraded.label: Model finding, downgraded because a stage was skipped
downgraded.caption: Pull request #17, 2026-09-26, job f2c676ba. For this run we cut the time budget to 150 seconds on purpose, to exercise this path. The third pass did not run, so the finding was downgraded to a warning, and the comment says why.

measurement.heading: One number, with its limits
measurement.result: 125 of 126 planted rule violations found, 0 false positives on 4 clean control fixtures.
measurement.method: Method: our rule-recall benchmark. We plant known violations in test fixtures and count one as found when the pre-scan or the model review reports the expected rule in the expected file.
measurement.run: Run: 2026-09-16, one full run. Models: Gemini 3.8 Flash for the review, Gemini 3.6 Flash for the blind re-check.
measurement.limits: Limits: we wrote the fixtures ourselves; these are not customer repositories. It is a single run, and results vary between runs. The benchmark runs without a time budget and without repository context, and it sends every fixture file to the model review. In production the model review reads only TypeScript and JavaScript files, and 69 of the 126 violations sit in other file types, which the model does not see in a real pull request. On a larger fixture with 48 planted violations (2026-09-29, two runs) the result was 46 of 48 both times. The model for the third pass has changed since this run.

pillarDeterministic.header: 55 rules are checked by code, not by a model.
pillarDeterministic.paragraphDetectors: The pre-scan runs before any model call. It uses pattern matchers, syntax-tree queries, config checks, lint rules and package-registry lookups, and it has a detector for 55 rule IDs.
pillarDeterministic.paragraphNoRejudge: A model never re-judges a deterministic finding. If the model reports the same rule at the same place, the deterministic finding wins. In the result it is marked deterministic.

pillarModel.header: A second model re-checks each finding without the first one’s reasoning.
pillarModel.paragraphDraft: The rule catalogue has 119 entries. Rules without a detector need judgement, so a model reviews the diff against the rules that apply to your stack. Some rules describe process and cannot be checked on a diff at all. What the model reports is a claim, not yet a finding.
pillarModel.paragraphBlind: A second model gets only the rule, the location, the quoted code and the diff. It does not see the first model’s explanation, severity or fix. It answers confirmed, refuted or uncertain. Refuted claims are removed. Uncertain ones, and critical ones that are refuted or weakly confirmed, get a third pass. What stays uncertain becomes a warning and says so.
pillarModel.paragraphHonest: Two things to know. All models are Gemini models from one vendor: the independence comes from what the second model is not shown, not from a different model family. And not every finding gets the blind re-check: large diffs can be reviewed in a single pass without it, and the review then says so.

pillarDegradation.header: A skipped stage is reported, not hidden.
pillarDegradation.paragraphBudget: Every review has a time budget of 300 seconds. When the re-check or the third pass cannot run because of time, a model error or an exhausted budget, the findings are not passed off as verified. A finding that was waiting for the third pass is downgraded to a warning with a note. If the re-check did not run, the confidence score reads n/a instead of a number.
pillarDegradation.paragraphNotice: The pull request, the check run and the CLI then carry the same line, for example: “Reduced confidence: time budget exhausted — skipped: blind verification (some or all findings).” If the model review fails on some files, those files are listed by name.
pillarDegradation.punchline: “Nothing was reviewed — this is NOT a clean verdict.”

verdictTable.heading: Which part of the verdict comes from where

rules.model: Rules that need judgement, from a catalogue of 119

production.prescan: Code: patterns, syntax tree, config checks, lint rules, registry lookups
production.model: One model drafts it, a second model re-checks it blind

files.prescan: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, Go, Rust, C and C++, plus config files such as YAML, JSON, Terraform and TOML

gate.prescan: Yes. A CRITICAL finding fails the check.
gate.model: Yes. A CRITICAL finding fails the check, so a verdict can rest on a model finding.

swallowedErrors.rebuttal: Because the error was caught and dropped. A catch block that logs and returns null looks tidy in a diff and hides the failure in production. The confirmed finding above is exactly this.

inventedPackages.rebuttal: The package name was made up. Unslop looks up the dependencies declared in package.json, requirements.txt, pyproject.toml and Cargo.toml on their registry (rule SEC-035).

greenTests.rebuttal: A test without an assertion is always green. Assertion-free tests are one of the deterministic rules (TEST-001).

unreadDiff.rebuttal: The agent changed more than anyone read. Unslop reviews every push to the pull request again and comments on the line in question.

architectureSpec.heading: One review, four surfaces
architectureSpec.intro: Pull request, terminal, editor, coding agent.

rules.definition: 119 rules, each with an ID. 55 have a deterministic detector. The model review is given the rules that apply to your stack; some rules describe process and cannot be checked on a diff.

enforcement.definition: GitHub App. Every review is a check run named “Anti-Slop Gatekeeper” plus comments on the lines. A CRITICAL finding fails the check; warnings conclude as neutral.

retrieval.definition: For connected repositories, signatures and type definitions from your code are retrieved as context for the model. They inform the review; they never excuse a rule violation.

rescans.definition: Each push to a pull request is reviewed on its own. There is no comparison with the previous revision.

integration.definition: “unslop scan” reviews your local changes against the merge-base and can apply suggested fixes. The VS Code extension shows findings as diagnostics. An MCP server offers the scan to coding agents. All three are built and not published yet.

webhooks.definition: Every GitHub webhook is verified by its HMAC-SHA256 signature.

tokens.definition: GitHub OAuth tokens are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. API keys are stored as hashes.

planned.definition: Not built yet: failing the check when a revision raises findings over the previous one, and a second model vendor for the re-check.

limits.definition: Nothing catches every flaw in AI-written code, and neither do we. The model review reads TypeScript and JavaScript only, and its results vary between runs.

sourceCode.question: Do you store or train on our source code?
sourceCode.answer: We don’t train on it, and neither does Google: the Vertex AI service terms exclude using customer prompts and responses to train Google’s models. The review models run on the EU multi-region endpoint of Vertex AI, for which Google guarantees that ML processing stays inside EU member states. For a pull request we read the diff and the changed files from GitHub for the review, and we store the findings with the quoted lines, not the diff. A scan from the CLI or the MCP server uploads a diff, and that diff is stored with the scan; before the upload, the client refuses any diff in which it detects a secret. The repository index is built from signatures, interfaces and type definitions rather than implementation logic. GitHub OAuth tokens are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM.

ciSpeed.question: Will this slow down our CI/CD or block our merges?
ciSpeed.answer: It runs next to your CI, not inside it. The webhook returns as soon as the review is registered; the review then runs as a GitHub check run with a hard limit of 300 seconds. Only CRITICAL findings fail the check; warnings conclude as neutral and do not block a merge. Whether the check is required is your branch-protection setting.

adoption.question: Does my team need to learn another dashboard?
adoption.answer: No. Findings appear as a check run and as review comments on the pull request. The CLI diffs your tracked changes against the merge-base, and the VS Code extension shows findings and applies suggested fixes in the editor; both are built and not published yet. The dashboard is for repositories, scan history, API keys and billing.

determinism.question: Is this just another AI reviewer?
determinism.answer: Partly, and we say which part. 55 rules are checked by deterministic detectors, and those findings never pass through a model. The rest is a model review, and a finding from it can fail the check. That is why a second model re-checks the findings without seeing the first one’s reasoning, and why the review states when that re-check did not happen. Model calls run at temperature 0; results still vary somewhat between runs.

languages.question: Which languages are covered?
languages.answer: The model review reads TypeScript and JavaScript files. The deterministic pre-scan also covers Python, Java, Go, Rust, C and C++ and common config files. Today a pull request is only reviewed if it contains at least one TypeScript or JavaScript file; otherwise the check concludes as neutral with “Nothing to review”.

outage.question: What happens when a review fails?
outage.answer: The check is closed, not left hanging. A failed review concludes as a failure with the reason in the check, for example “Review timed out”. A review that is not started (no subscription, quota used up, repository deactivated) posts a completed check with the conclusion “action required” that says why. If you made the check required, GitHub’s branch-protection overrides still apply.
